title: The heart and the rest of the fetus: extracardiac anomalies

items.question: About how often are extracardiac anomalies found in infants with congenital heart disease?
options: Up to 20%
Almost never
In every infant
Only in infants with a chromosomal abnormality
items.explanation: Up to 20% of infants have an extracardiac anomaly. The proportion is higher in fetuses.

items.question: Is the proportion with extracardiac anomalies higher in fetuses or in infants?
options: Higher in fetuses, with figures up to 50% to 70% reported
Higher in infants
The same in both
Not known in either
items.explanation: Fetal series report higher proportions, up to 50% to 70%.

items.question: Which pair of lesions is more often isolated?
options: D-transposition and pulmonary atresia with intact septum
Ventricular septal defect and tricuspid atresia
Ventricular septal defect and D-transposition
Tricuspid atresia and pulmonary atresia with intact septum
items.explanation: Ventricular septal defect and tricuspid atresia are often associated with other anomalies. D-transposition and pulmonary atresia with intact septum are more often isolated.

items.question: A fetus is diagnosed with heart disease. What survey is recommended?
options: A detailed survey of all fetal anatomy by an expert operator
A survey only if the heart disease is complex
No survey, because the heart explains the findings
A survey only at birth
items.explanation: A detailed anatomy survey is recommended for every fetus with heart disease, and repeat assessment may be appropriate.

items.question: The first detailed survey of a fetus with heart disease is normal outside the heart. What follows?
options: Repeat assessment may be appropriate, because some anomalies are only detectable later
The survey never needs repeating
Extracardiac anomalies can be excluded for good
Only a postnatal check is allowed
items.explanation: Some anomalies may only be detectable later, so repeat assessment may be appropriate.
